slides.0.title: Geography, Climate and Viticulture
slides.0.subtitle: Sun, mountains and island winds
slides.1.title: Four climate zones
slides.1.highlights.0.title: North: temperate to continental
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Cold winters, possible snow and more rainfall
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Central Greece: moderated Mediterranean
slides.1.highlights.2.title: South and Peloponnese: hot and stable
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Hot, dry summers with little vintage variation
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Aegean islands: arid and windy
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Strong sea winds and minimal rainfall; the sea moderates temperature
slides.1.content: Greece is often taught as four climate zones, though altitude and sea breezes cause large differences within a zone.
slides.2.title: Mountains and altitude
slides.2.highlights.0.title: A mountainous country
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Around 80% of vineyards are mountainous or semi-mountainous
slides.2.highlights.1.title: From sea level to over 1,000 m
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Vineyards span a huge altitude range
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Altitude preserves acidity
slides.2.highlights.2.content: In a hot climate, high sites are chosen deliberately to keep acidity and aroma
slides.2.content: Example: Moschofilero on the roughly 660 m Mantinia plateau is often harvested only in mid-October.
slides.3.title: Soils and terroir
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Santorini: volcanic ash and pumice
slides.3.highlights.0.content: From the Minoan eruption around 1600 BCE; nutrient-poor
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Naoussa: limestone clay and marl
slides.3.highlights.1.content: The core soil for northern Xinomavro
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Rapsani: schist
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Attica: calcareous soils
slides.3.content: Soil is only part of terroir; in Diploma essays discuss soil, altitude, wind and grape together.
slides.4.title: Viticultural traditions
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Santorini's kouloura
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Vines woven low into baskets protect the fruit from fierce wind and sun
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Phylloxera-free
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Santorini's volcanic pumice and ash soils are phylloxera-free, so grafted rootstocks are not needed
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Dry farming
slides.4.highlights.2.content: With limited water, Santorini is dry-farmed
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Bush-vine training
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Many old vines are bush-trained: low-yielding and drought-tolerant
slides.4.content: These practices answer wind, drought and poor soil; they are not just "tradition".
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
Why choose high-altitude vineyards in a hot climate?
B. To keep acidity and aroma
Altitude cools nights and lengthens ripening, helping keep acidity and aroma.
A. A type of oak barrel
B. A training method weaving vines into low baskets
Kouloura tucks the fruit inside the basket, shielding it from wind and sun.
Why does Santorini not need grafted rootstocks?
A. The climate is too cold
B. Its volcanic pumice and ash soils are phylloxera-free
C. It is banned by law
This is a much-cited Santorini feature, which together with old vines and dry farming underpins its style.
